Physiological mechanisms {#sec-hrr-mechanisms}

The decrease of HR after exercise results from changes in the autonomic control of the heart [@pecanha2014]. Two mechanisms act with different time courses:

Parasympathetic (vagal) reactivation mainly drives the early, fast decrease of HR. It is triggered by the deactivation of central command and of the mechanoreflex as soon as the exercise stops [@pecanha2014; @imai1994]. Sympathetic withdrawal mainly drives the later, slow decrease of HR. It is linked to the progressive deactivation of the metaboreflex and of thermoregulatory mechanisms [@pecanha2014].

These pathways are impaired in cardiovascular diseases, which explains the slower recovery observed in these patients and its association with mortality [@cole1999; @pecanha2014].

Expected characteristics of the recovery curve {#sec-hrr-curve}

From the literature, the recovery curve should show:

A fast initial decrease during the first tens of seconds, related to vagal reactivation, which is the period described by T30 [@imai1994]. A slower decrease afterwards, related to sympathetic withdrawal [@pecanha2014]. A progressive flattening of the curve towards an asymptotic value, $\mathrm{HR}_\infty$, rather than a constant rate of decrease. A dependence on exercise intensity: after maximal exercise, the time constant of a mono-exponential fit is unstable and only stabilises after about 3 minutes of recording [@pierpont2000]. Is one model sufficient for the whole recovery? {#sec-hrr-one-model}

The literature suggests that a single mono-exponential model is not always sufficient. HRR has been described as an exponential curve with a fast and a slow decay component [@pecanha2014]. A first-order exponential decay was found adequate after submaximal exercise but inadequate after maximal exercise, with non-random residuals [@pierpont2000]. After maximal exercise, a double-exponential model fitted the recovery better than a single exponential in 22 of 36 participants, with a short time constant ($\tau_1 \approx 44$ s) and a longer one ($\tau_2 \approx 120$ s) [@joseph2023]. The choice of model therefore depends on the exercise intensity and on the duration of the recorded recovery.

Our hypotheses {#sec-hrr-hypotheses}

Based on this literature, we formulate the following hypotheses for the two recordings:

H1: The linear model will give the poorest fit, with structured (curved) residuals, because the decrease of HR is not constant over time. H2: On the 7.5-minute recording, a mono-exponential model may be sufficient if the preceding exercise was submaximal, but its residuals may remain structured if the exercise was close to maximal [@pierpont2000]. H3: On the 3-hour recording, a bi-exponential model will describe the recovery better than a mono-exponential model, with a fast component (time constant of tens of seconds) and a slow component (time constant of minutes), reflecting vagal reactivation and sympathetic withdrawal [@pecanha2014; @joseph2023]. H4: The added complexity of the bi-exponential model will only be justified if it clearly improves the fit and removes the structure of the residuals.
